passage: At the school's Saturday hobby club, Shankar from class seven had a shiny sheet of football stickers. "Fifty rupees," he said. Madhav gasped. That was nearly all his pocket money. "Forty?" "Forty-five." "Forty!" Shankar sighed dramatically and agreed. Madhav ran to the art table, grinning, and told his friend he'd saved ten whole rupees. The friend looked at the sheet. "The stationery shop outside the gate sells these for twenty." Madhav's smile wobbled. "But he said fifty first," he said slowly, as if that settled it. For the rest of the club hour he kept smoothing the sheet, not quite sure whether he had won or lost.

qa.q: What price did Shankar name first?
qa.a: Shankar first said fifty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Madhav feel he had saved ten rupees?
qa.a: Madhav treated fifty as the real price because it was the first number he heard, so paying forty felt like a win even though the shop charged twenty.

qa.q: What could Madhav try before the next swap or sale?
qa.a: He could first check what the stationery shop charges and decide his own top price before hearing any seller's number.

qa.q: How might Shankar see the bargain?
qa.a: Shankar probably feels pleased; starting at fifty made forty look generous, and he still earned double the shop price.

grounding: Shows a child treating a seller's first sticker price as the fair baseline, so a smaller but still high price feels like a big win.

passage: Every Sunday a man sets up a sticker cart outside our building, and last week I watched Devika, the eight-year-old from the second floor, bargain with him. I'm Manjula, Manju aunty to the children here, and I was buying coriander nearby. "Unicorn sheet, sixty rupees," he told her. Her eyebrows shot up. She offered forty; he said fifty-five; they settled at fifty. She skipped back past me, whispering, "I got ten off!" I didn't say anything. The same sheet was taped to the side of the cart with a faded price tag: 30. Maybe she saw it, maybe she didn't. She looked so proud that I wasn't sure what to tell her.

qa.q: What price was on the faded tag taped to the cart?
qa.a: The faded price tag on the cart said 30.

qa.q: Why was Devika so proud of the deal?
qa.a: The first price of sixty set the scale in her mind, so fifty felt like a real win; she didn't compare it with what the sheet was actually worth.

qa.q: How could Manjula help Devika without spoiling her happiness?
qa.a: Manjula could later walk with her to look at the tag and ask, playfully, what she would offer next time if she saw the tag first. That turns it into a game rather than a scolding. 🙂

qa.q: What is it like for Manjula to watch the bargain?
qa.a: Manjula feels torn: she saw the tag and wants to help, but Devika is so happy that speaking up feels unkind.

grounding: Shows a child treating the seller's first price of sixty as the baseline, so fifty feels like a big win though the tag says thirty.

passage:
Monday: At recess, Mohit fanned out his spare cricket stickers. "Rare ones. Hundred rupees each." Divyansh swallowed. A hundred! He went home and counted his coin box twice.
Wednesday: "Seventy?" Divyansh tried. "Eighty," said Mohit. "Sixty-five, final." They shook hands. Divyansh walked around the playground all afternoon feeling like a businessman; he'd knocked off thirty-five rupees.
Saturday: At the paper shop with Dadi, Divyansh saw the same stickers in packets of five for forty rupees. He stood there doing sums on his fingers. "I paid sixty-five for one," he said quietly. Dadi asked why. "Because he said a hundred first, and sixty-five sounded small."

qa.q: How much did a packet of five stickers cost at the paper shop?
qa.a: A packet of five stickers cost forty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh feel like a businessman on Wednesday?
qa.a: He measured the deal against Mohit's first price of a hundred, so getting it down to sixty-five felt like a clever saving of thirty-five rupees.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do the next time someone names a price first?
qa.a: He could say he'll think about it and check the shop price before bargaining, so his own checking, not the seller's number, sets the start.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel hearing Divyansh explain what happened?
qa.a: Dadi might feel a little sorry about the lost money but pleased that he worked out the reason on his own.

grounding: Shows a child anchored on a classmate's first sticker price, feeling a lower but still high price is a win, and later noticing why.

passage: Abhinav, you think you're a good bargainer? Let me tell you about your Dada at nine, in Bhopal, 1968. At the Muharram fair a boy had a tin box of glittery animal stickers. I asked the price. "Two rupees for the tiger," he said. Two rupees! My whole pocket money for a month was three. I said, "One rupee." He said, "One-fifty, final." I felt I'd beaten him. I, Yusuf, walked off holding that tiger like a trophy. At the next stall a man was selling the same tigers. Four annas each. Four annas! I stood there with my mouth open. That boy had simply picked a big number first, and I had bargained down from his number, not from what the tiger was worth.

qa.q: How much did the boy first ask for the tiger sticker?
qa.a: Two rupees for the tiger.

qa.q: Why did young Yusuf feel he had beaten the boy?
qa.a: He measured the deal against the two rupees he first heard, so one rupee fifty felt like a big saving. He didn't know the real price, so the first number felt like the fair one.

qa.q: What could Yusuf have done at the fair before paying?
qa.a: He could have walked around the other stalls first to see what the same stickers cost, so he had his own idea of a fair price.

qa.q: How might the boy with the tin box have felt as Yusuf walked away?
qa.a: He was probably pleased, since his big opening price had worked and he got far more than the stickers sold for next door.

grounding: A grandfather recalls bargaining for a sticker as a boy, treating the seller's first high price as the baseline and feeling he'd won.

passage: The church-yard jumble sale in Kochi was closing in ten minutes, and rain had started on the tarpaulins. Noor, nine, clutched sixty rupees and stopped at the table where a teenager called Thomas was selling a sticker album of space rockets. "How much?" "Three hundred." Noor's stomach dropped. Three hundred was impossible. "Can I have it for… a hundred and fifty?" "Two hundred." "A hundred?" The rain got louder. Thomas started folding his tablecloth. "Fine. Last price, eighty." Noor felt she was winning big. Eighty was so much less than three hundred! She borrowed twenty from her cousin and paid, grinning. On the way home, her cousin said quietly, "That album is thirty in the bookshop near school." Noor looked at the wet album and said nothing for a while.

qa.q: How much did Thomas first ask for the sticker album?
qa.a: Three hundred.

qa.q: Why did eighty rupees feel like a big win to Noor?
qa.a: Noor felt thrilled because she compared eighty with the three hundred she heard first, so it seemed tiny. The rain and closing time also rushed her, leaving no chance to think about the real price.

qa.q: With the sale closing and rain starting, what could Noor have tried instead?
qa.a: She could have asked her cousin what such albums usually cost, or decided her own top price before hearing any number, and walked away if it was higher.

qa.q: How might Noor's cousin have felt lending her twenty rupees?
qa.a: The cousin may have felt uneasy watching the deal and waited until afterwards to say something gently, not wanting to spoil the moment in the rain.

grounding: A girl at a closing jumble sale bargains down from a high first price and feels she has won, though the final price is still too high.

passage: At the Shivratri fair in their kasba, Pradeep stopped at a stall hung with shiny cricket stickers. "Fifty rupees for the sheet," said the stall man. Pradeep gasped, then remembered how his uncle bargained. "Forty!" The man shook his head. "Thirty-five, last price." "Done!" Pradeep handed over the coins Nani had given him and skipped back to his sister Aditi. "I saved fifteen rupees!" Aditi looked at the sheet, then at him. "Chintu at school sells these for twenty." Pradeep's grin wobbled. "But he said fifty first. Thirty-five is way less than fifty." "Less than fifty, sure," said Aditi. "Not less than twenty." Pradeep stared at his stickers, suddenly not so sure they were shiny.

qa.q: What price did Pradeep finally pay for the sticker sheet?
qa.a: He paid thirty-five rupees.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep feel he had got a great deal?
qa.a: He felt proud and excited because thirty-five looked small next to the first price of fifty, so it felt like saving fifteen rupees.

qa.q: What could Pradeep try at the next stall?
qa.a: Before hearing the seller's price, he could remember what the same thing costs at school and bargain from that number instead.

qa.q: How does Aditi see Pradeep's bargain?
qa.a: She sees that he still paid more than the school price, and points out that thirty-five is only cheap when compared with fifty.

grounding: At a fair, a boy treats a seller's first price as the fair level, so a still-high price feels like a big saving.

passage: At recess in their school in Porto, Paulo finally spotted it: the shiny goalkeeper sticker he needed to finish his album page. Chen, a year older, held it up. "Ten of your stickers for this one." Ten! Paulo's stomach dropped. He only had twelve spares. "Seven?" he tried. Chen pretended to think. "Eight, and that's me being nice." Paulo counted out eight and hurried away, glowing. "I got him down by two!" he told his friend Tiago. Tiago frowned. "Shinies go for three. Everyone knows that. Beatriz traded one for three yesterday." Paulo looked at his thin stack of four spares. Eight had felt like winning because it wasn't ten. Now it just felt like eight.

qa.q: How many spare stickers did Paulo have left after the trade?
qa.a: He had four spares left.

qa.q: Why was Paulo glowing after the trade?
qa.a: He felt triumphant because he had talked Chen down from ten, so eight felt like a win even though it was far above the usual price.

qa.q: What small step would help Paulo before his next trade?
qa.a: Ask a couple of friends what shinies usually go for, and decide his own fair number before hearing Chen's.

qa.q: How might Chen see the trade?
qa.a: Chen probably feels pleased, since starting at ten brought in eight, far more than the usual three.

grounding: In a playground sticker swap, a boy treats an older child's first asking number as the baseline, so a still-high trade feels like a win.

passage: On Children's Day the school hall turned into a fair, and everything cost coupons. Gautam, in class five, stopped at the Class Nine stall where Abhinav was selling glittery sticker packs. "Twenty coupons," Abhinav announced. Gautam had fifteen. "Twelve?" "Eighteen." "Fourteen, please, bhaiya." Abhinav sighed loudly. "Fine, fourteen, only for you." Gautam ran to his class teacher, waving the pack. "Ma'am! I got it six coupons cheaper!" Ms Kurian turned it over. "The same packs are at the Class Seven stall for eight coupons," she said. Gautam's face fell. "But he said twenty." "He did," she said. "And after twenty, fourteen sounds tiny, doesn't it?" Gautam looked at the one coupon left in his hand.

qa.q: How many coupons did Gautam pay for the sticker pack?
qa.a: He paid fourteen coupons.

qa.q: Why was Gautam so pleased when he ran to his teacher?
qa.a: He felt proud because fourteen seemed six coupons cheaper than Abhinav's twenty, so it felt like a big win.

qa.q: What could Gautam do at the next fair before buying?
qa.a: He could walk round and see what the same thing costs at other stalls first, so the first number he hears doesn't become his guide.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see the deal?
qa.a: Abhinav probably knew twenty was high and was pleased to get fourteen while making it sound like a favour.

grounding: At a school fair, a boy bargains down from a senior's first price and feels he won, though the same pack sells for far less elsewhere.

passage:
Monday. At school in Bhopal, an older boy offered Wasim a sheet of shiny dinosaur stickers. "Fifty rupees." Wasim gasped. Fifty was a lot. He only had twenty in his pocket.

Wednesday. Wasim asked his sister Sunaina for money. "He'll give it for thirty now! I bargained!" He was so proud. Twenty whole rupees less! Sunaina frowned. "Thirty for one sheet of stickers?" "It was fifty!" Wasim said. She gave him ten, still frowning.

Saturday. At the stationery shop near the market, Wasim saw the same dinosaur stickers on a hook. The price tag said ten rupees. He stared. He counted on his fingers. He had paid thirty. He felt his face go hot. "But he said fifty," he whispered to Sunaina. She put an arm around him. "That's why he said fifty first."

qa.q: How much did the stickers cost at the stationery shop?
qa.a: Ten rupees.

qa.q: Why did Wasim feel proud paying thirty rupees?
qa.a: The first price of fifty stuck in his mind, so thirty felt like a big win, even though it was still too high.

qa.q: What could Wasim do next time someone names a price?
qa.a: He could check the price in a shop first, or ask Sunaina, before deciding if a deal is fair.

qa.q: How does Sunaina seem to feel when Wasim sees the ten-rupee tag?
qa.a: Sunaina seems sympathetic and gentle, putting an arm around him instead of saying 'I told you so'.

grounding: It shows a child who treats the first price he hears as the fair baseline, so a lower but still high price feels like a win, over several days.

passage: Elizabeth, you want to know why I always ask the price in three shops? Let me tell you about the Lepcha stall at the Darjeeling mela when I was ten. A man had these beautiful glass marbles, blue with white swirls. I asked, "How much?" He said, "Thirty rupees for five." That was huge then. I bargained, and he came down to twenty. I felt like the cleverest girl in the hills. I ran to show my Ama. She looked at the marbles and laughed. "Dolma, the shop by the monastery sells ten for ten rupees." I didn't believe her. We walked there. She was right. I cried the whole way home. It wasn't the money. It was that I had felt so clever. The first number had tricked me into thinking twenty was cheap.

qa.q: What did the man first say the marbles cost?
qa.a: Thirty rupees for five.

qa.q: Why did young Dolma feel so clever after bargaining to twenty?
qa.a: The first price of thirty made twenty feel like a big win, so Dolma felt proud even though the marbles were still overpriced.

qa.q: At what point in the story could Dolma have avoided being tricked?
qa.a: Before bargaining, she could have checked other stalls like the shop by the monastery to know what a fair price was.

qa.q: How might Dolma's Ama have felt when her daughter cried on the way home?
qa.a: Ama may have felt tender and a bit sorry, knowing the lesson hurt but would stay with her.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a child, the first price she heard made a still-high price feel like a win.

passage: The school fair in Jaipur closed at five, and Disha, nine, had only ten minutes left and forty rupees from Papa. At the last stall, a big girl was selling sticker books. "Eighty rupees." Disha's heart sank. "Please, I only have forty." The girl sighed dramatically. "Okay, okay. Fifty." Disha begged. "Forty-five, final." Disha ran to borrow five rupees from her friend Raghav, who was eating candyfloss. "Quick! She came down from eighty!" Raghav handed over five. Disha bought the book, grinning. "I saved thirty-five rupees!" she told everyone. On the way home, Raghav flipped through it. "It says twenty on the back," he said, pointing to the printed price. Disha looked. Twenty. She had felt so clever. Now she felt her cheeks burn.

qa.q: What price was printed on the back of the sticker book?
qa.a: Twenty.

qa.q: Why did Disha feel she had saved thirty-five rupees?
qa.a: The first price of eighty stuck in her mind, so forty-five felt like a huge discount and she felt clever, even though it was more than double the printed price.

qa.q: What could Disha try next time at a stall?
qa.a: She could look for a printed price or ask a friend what things usually cost before bargaining from the seller's number.

grounding: It shows a child who treats the first price as the fair baseline, so a lower number feels like a big win even when it's still too high.

passage:
Christmas week in Bandra, and the lane outside St Peter's was strung with paper stars. Jaya had saved forty rupees for the sticker stall that Deepika, a Class 7 girl, ran from a shoebox.

"The glitter unicorn is thirty," Deepika said.

Thirty! Jaya's heart sank.

"Twenty-five?" Jaya tried.

"Okay, twenty-five, since it's Christmas."

Jaya skipped home, feeling clever. She'd saved five whole rupees!

At home her brother looked at the sticker. "They sell those at the stationery shop for ten."

It had felt like such a good deal. Twenty-five was so much less than thirty. But it was still more than twice what it cost at the shop.

She stuck it in her notebook anyway. But next time, she decided, she'd check the shop first.

qa.q: How much did the stationery shop sell the sticker for?
qa.a: They sell those at the stationery shop for ten.

qa.q: Why did Jaya feel so clever after paying twenty-five?
qa.a: Jaya felt pleased and proud because twenty-five seemed like a big win compared with Deepika's first price of thirty.

qa.q: What did Jaya decide to do next time, and why is that wise?
qa.a: Jaya decided to check the shop first, so she knows a fair price before hearing someone else's number.

qa.q: How might Deepika have seen the bargaining?
qa.a: Deepika may have felt pleased with her sale, knowing thirty was a high starting price that made twenty-five look generous.

grounding: A child bargaining for a sticker treats the first price as fair and feels she won, though the price is still too high.

passage:
"Ritu didi, how much for the tiger sticker?"

"For you? Fifty."

"FIFTY? It's Durga Puja, didi, be kind."

"Fine. Forty."

"Thirty?"

"Thirty-five, final."

"Deal! I saved fifteen!"

Chaitanya handed over the coins from his pandal money and ran off to show his friends.

"Ma, I got the tiger sticker for thirty-five instead of fifty!"

Ma turned to Ritu. "How much did your sticker book cost?"

"...Sixty. For thirty stickers."

"So each one was two rupees."

"Ma!"

Chaitanya's face went blank. "But I bargained. It was fifty."

"It was fifty because she said fifty first," Ma said gently. "After that, everything smaller looked cheap."

"Didi, give me back my money!"

"Twenty-five back, and you keep the tiger?"

"...Thirty."

Ma laughed. "Now he's learning."

qa.q: How much did Ritu's sticker book cost?
qa.a: Sixty. For thirty stickers.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya feel he had saved fifteen?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt proud and excited, because thirty-five seemed far below the first price of fifty, even though that price was made up.

qa.q: What did Ma explain, and how can Chaitanya use it?
qa.a: Ma explained that fifty only mattered because it was said first; next time Chaitanya can ask what things really cost before bargaining.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel when Ma asks about the book's cost?
qa.a: Ritu might feel caught out and a bit sheepish, but also amused, since she offers some money back.

grounding: A child treats his sister's first sticker price as the baseline and feels he won, until his mother points out the real cost.

passage:
I'm Shankar. During the Onam holidays, my cousin Parul brought a big album of football stickers to Ammamma's house.

I wanted the goalkeeper one. "Twenty rupees," she said.

I only had twelve. We argued on the veranda beside the pookalam. Finally she said, "Okay, fifteen. Last price." I gave her my twelve and promised three more later.

I felt like a champion. I told everyone I got it for fifteen, not twenty!

Then my uncle said the packets at the Kochi shop have five stickers for ten rupees. Two rupees each.

I kept thinking: fifteen felt so small next to twenty. But twenty was just the first number Parul said. It wasn't real.

I still like the goalkeeper. But now when someone says a price, I remember that album.

qa.q: How much money did Shankar have?
qa.a: Shankar only had twelve.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel after getting the sticker for fifteen?
qa.a: Shankar felt like a champion, proud to have brought the price down from twenty.

qa.q: What did Shankar learn that could help in the next trade?
qa.a: Shankar learned that the first number isn't the real value, so checking what things usually cost first is wiser.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt when the uncle mentioned the shop price?
qa.a: Parul might have felt a little embarrassed, since the twenty-rupee price was clearly far above the real cost.

grounding: A child treats the first sticker price as fair and feels like a winner, then learns the real price was far lower.

passage:
Teacher's note, school Christmas fair — Elizabeth
Jaya, Class 3, went to the sticker stall run by the Class 7 children. The older girl told her, "Fifty rupees for this sheet." Jaya said, "Too much!" The girl said, "Okay, thirty." Jaya's face lit up. She paid at once and ran to me, delighted: "I got twenty rupees off!"
Two stalls down, the same sticker sheets were ten rupees each. Jaya saw them on her way back and went very quiet. "But she said fifty first," she said. "Thirty was a lot less."
I didn't scold her. I sat with her and we talked about how the first number we hear can make everything after it seem cheap or dear.
Next step: on Monday, in maths, the class will play a shop game where they look at all the stalls before choosing.

qa.q: What price did the older girl first say for the sticker sheet?
qa.a: She first said fifty rupees.

qa.q: Why did thirty rupees feel like a big win to Jaya?
qa.a: She felt delighted because the first price of fifty made thirty seem cheap, even though it was still more than the other stall.

qa.q: What did the teacher plan, and why is it a good countermeasure?
qa.a: A shop game where children look at all the stalls before choosing, so they compare real prices instead of judging from the first number.

qa.q: How might the older girl at the stall see the bargain?
qa.a: She probably felt pleased, since starting at fifty let her sell at thirty while Jaya felt she had won.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, a child treating the first sticker price as the fair baseline, so a lower price felt like a win though it was still too high.
